topic: Ollama coding agent: Qwen 3.8 27B mxfp8, OpenCode harness, sbx sandbox, context capped at 64K, on one laptop
title: Three installs and your Mac runs a coding agent tonight
hook_candidates: Thirty-two gigabytes. That's the whole model, on your laptop.
You've tried local models. Tonight one writes your code.
You've got one laptop. It can be your coding agent.
Three installs and your Mac runs a coding agent tonight.
A coding agent with no cloud, no key, no subscription.
Sixty-four thousand tokens. That's the cap that saves your laptop.
Your laptop isn't too small. The context window was uncapped.
Qwen 3.8 runs your agent. Ollama serves it. sbx cages it.
No API key. Your forty-eight-gigabyte Mac is the datacenter.
One developer front-paged the whole setup. Here's the stack.
narration_full: Three installs and your Mac runs a coding agent tonight. A coding agent reads your files, runs commands and edits code. You've watched cloud agents, never your own project. Move one: install the three tools. Ollama, a free server that runs models behind one command. OpenCode, the open source agent that lives in your terminal. S B X, Docker's sandbox, a small virtual machine the agent is locked inside. This recipe comes from a walkthrough written on a MacBook Pro with forty-eight gigabytes of memory. That laptop is the whole datacenter. Move two: pull the model. One command pulls the twenty-seven-billion-parameter Qwen, a coding model built for agent work, thirty-two gigabytes on disk. The download takes a while. It only happens once. The model fits because of M X F P eight, a quantization storing each weight as an eight-bit number. Each small block of weights gets its own scaling factor. You lose a little accuracy. For coding help, you will not feel it. Memory has a second tenant: the context window, the model's working memory, measured in tokens, chunks of text. Every file the agent reads sits inside it, and it grows with every word. On a machine this size, Ollama's default context is generous. Unchecked, it eats the headroom and locks the laptop. Move three: cap the context, then cage the agent. In OpenCode's config, set the model to sixty-five thousand tokens of context. Also drop reasoning effort, the hidden thinking, to low. The cap is the difference between a slow agent and a locked laptop. Ollama's own docs back the number. Now the cage: one folder, an S B X kit pointing the agent at your local Ollama. Run it, and OpenCode works inside its own filesystem and network. A hallucinated command dies in the sandbox, not on your machine. The honest catch. It runs slower than a paid cloud model, and the community argues about Ollama itself. We have not timed this exact stack. The trade: no A P I key, and your code never leaves the laptop. Then it is running. OpenCode edits your project while the Qwen thinks on your own hardware, caged and capped. Three installs, and tonight your Mac is the agent's whole datacenter.
